Well, Mr. Speaker, there has been a great deal of talk on the part of the opposition on the right to scrutiny and the right to debate. I suggest in all sincerity-and I am speaking more I think of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre than the official opposition-what they are really concerned with is not the right to scrutinize and not the right to debate; they are concerned with the right to obstruct and the right to blockade.
They have discovered that procedure can be used-as it was used by the Irish members in the mid 19th century in Great Britain-to blockade the government. If that had not been so, if they were concerned simply with debate and a full discussion of the issues, why did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre not accept the suggestion of the government house leader for unlimited debate and discussion in the committees? That would have given time for a full discussion of the issue and would have given time to arouse the press and the public. I suggest the reason he did not want the debate in committee and wanted unlimited debate in the house instead was because he knew that unlimited debate in the house would block not simply one piece of legislation but the whole government program. That is what he wanted-to blockade the house. He does not want simply to blockade one piece of legislation. He does not want simply to debate it to arouse the country. He wants a pistol at the head of the government. He wants a weapon to use as an exercise in political blackmail, a quid pro quo for the government bending to the opposition.
Our task, Mr. Speaker, I think is not simply to discuss and debate in parliament. Our task is to make parliament pertinent to the needs of the nation. When listening to members of the opposition I was reminded of a statement made only two years ago by a Conservative member in this house-

I say that is still true. I say the people of Canada are sick and tired of parliamentary tricks and treats as played by so many members of the opposition. The basic question is how much time for debate is reasonable and who should decide this. I admit freely to the house, and I said so at the time, that the provision called 16a presented by the government last December was not a provision I could support. I would not because I did not think the balance it presented was fair. I am convinced, however, that the present allocation is a fair one which corresponds to our age of telecommunications. It may be that one day in the past, in the horse and buggy days, it required weeks and months of debate so that members could go back to their constituents and bring home to them the matters of concern. That is not true in an age when you can send in seconds a signal to the moon. It is not true when we have, as we do now, television, radio and newspapers nation-wide and responsive in bringing home to the public issues of public concern. Ten days delay and four days debate are sufficient in communicating to the public if the issue is one of genuine, serious and important concern.
Some of the best debates-those on urgent matters-are short. They take only one day.
But they capture more press and public attention than long winded efforts.
I suggest that the people of Canada do not want simply a debate; they do not want repetitious, time wasting, sterile, fractious, carping. They want action. What the opposition wants is the ability to close off action and to obtain indirectly the power which the voters denied them directly. They want to be able to talk forever-to talk legislation to death. I have some news, for members of the opposition. There are many people in this country who are not as fond of hearing members of this house as some of the members are of hearing themselves.

The public want a House of Commons which will wallow less and do more. They do not want a web of words, a cocoon of parliamentary technicalities from which no butterflies of legislation fly.
In closing, perhaps it would be appropriate for me to mention the Leader of the Opposition who has been rising periodically in this house with a voice of doom, stretching out his wavering hand and saying, "In all honesty can you as a member of this house support this measure?" I will save the Leader of the Opposition that dramatic gesture. Let me say to the Leader of the Opposition that the best is sometimes the enemy of the good. Nothing under God's sun is perfect. But this is a good proposal and I support it unreservedly.
